scenes.name: a few fast workers, thousands of slow ones
scenes.visual: Opens on the previous chapter's 30 ms bar, redrawn on its own on an empty canvas (no title, no teal arrows): 1,500 px wide, with its 5 px amber sliver 'arithmetic, under 1%' and the coral remainder carrying a coral tag with a blank name box and a '?'. The bar shrinks to a small parked copy at the top-right corner (about 300 px wide, coral remainder and '?' tag still visible) and stays there, dimmed, for the whole scene. The rest of the canvas splits into two horizontal bands with a faint grey divider. Top band, the CPU: four large blue rounded cards in a row, each with a worker icon (Phosphor 'user-gear'), label 'CPU' at the left. Bottom band, the GPU: a dense grid of small amber squares, 48 columns by 12 rows (576 drawn, standing for thousands), label 'GPU' at the left. Both bands persist. Amber '×' task tiles are later poured into both, so the grid visibly swallows a whole batch in one go while the four cards queue. The grid then briefly becomes a pixel screen, and a chain of blue token pills shows the one shape of work this chip is bad at. Colour: blue for the CPU cards and token pills (structure), amber for the GPU grid and the multiplications (arithmetic).

beats.say: So what fills the coral ninety-nine percent? Start with the chip.
beats.show: The 30 ms bar fades up centre on an empty canvas: 1,500 px wide, the 5 px amber sliver labelled 'arithmetic, under 1%', and the coral '?' name tag from the previous chapter fading back onto the coral remainder. No title, no teal arrows. On 'the coral ninety-nine percent', the coral part pulses once and the '?' tag brightens. On 'Start with the chip', the bar shrinks to the top-right corner and parks there, dimmed, still coral with its '?'. The empty top and bottom bands draw in with the faint divider between them.

beats.say: A laptop's processor, a C P U, is a few fast workers, each clever and quick to switch tasks.
beats.show: A laptop icon appears at the top-left and the four blue worker cards slide out of it into the top band. Label 'CPU', caption 'a few fast workers'. On 'quick to switch tasks', each card's small task icon flicks through a calculator, an envelope, a folder and a globe, each card out of step with the others.

beats.say: A graphics processing unit, a G P U, is thousands of slow, plain ones, all doing the same thing at once to different numbers.
beats.show: Bottom band: the amber grid fills in row by row from the left. Label 'GPU', caption 'thousands of slow ones'. On 'the same thing at once', every square pulses together, in unison, while the four top cards keep doing different things out of step.

beats.say: A token is about seventy billion multiplications, in huge batches where none waits on another, so a G P U clears thousands at a time.
beats.show: Centre overlay, both bands dimmed: a pile of identical amber '×' tiles, and a counter beside it running to '≈ 70,000,000,000 multiplications per token' on 'seventy billion'. On 'huge batches', the pile separates into a column of stacked trays of tiles, one tray standing for one batch; grey tag 'within a batch, no tile waits' and, smaller beneath it, 'named next chapter: vector × matrix'. As the two tags fade, on 'clears thousands', the top tray splits in two streams: top, tiles queue in front of the four cards, which take four at a time while a long queue grows; bottom, tiles rain onto the grid, one per square, and the whole grid flashes and clears them together, again and again. Right-edge counters: top 'cleared: 4, 8, 12', bottom 'cleared: 576, 1,152, 1,728'. Grey corner tag 'schematic'.

beats.say: The graphics in its name is historical: colouring pixels is the same shape of work. Its weakness is chains, each step needing the last, like writing one token at a time.
beats.show: Queues clear. On 'graphics', the label 'GPU' at the left of the bottom band expands briefly to 'graphics processing unit' and back. On 'colouring pixels', the grid morphs into a monitor icon full of pixels, label '1920 × 1080 ≈ 2 million pixels', every pixel lighting at the same instant, then morphs back into the grid. On 'chains', five blue token pills appear over the bottom band joined by arrows; pill 1 lights, then pill 2 only after pill 1 is done, then 3, 4, 5, while all but one square of the grid sit dark. Grey tags: 'each waits for the last' and, smaller, 'returns later'.

beats.say: Not chosen for cleverness, then, but because the workload is a vast number of identical, independent multiplications, the one thing it's good at.
beats.show: The chain fades. The amber grid brightens to full width while the four blue cards dim. Heading over the grid: 'not chosen for cleverness'. Three words land beneath it as they are spoken: 'vast', 'identical', 'independent'.

scenes.name: the arithmetic and the numbers live apart
scenes.visual: The GPU package illustration, centred and large: an amber compute die at centre-left, coral memory blocks on the right, and between them a bus of many thin parallel lines. Above the die 'The chip', above the memory 'The memory'. A small grey tag at the package's lower-left corner reads 'generic GPU'; no stack count and no chip name are shown, because this package stands for any GPU. It is named 'H100 · 80 GB' only when it returns in scene 10. Coral weight tiles flow across the bus from memory to die, where each flashes amber for an instant as it is used. A token counter at the top-centre ticks as the whole flow repeats. The previous chapter's bar stays parked small at the top-right; in this scene its blank coral tag is finally filled. This package is the chapter's reference image and returns in later scenes.

beats.say: From now on, the chip means the G P U's compute die, the part that calculates. It holds only about a thousandth of the model.
beats.show: The amber grid from the last scene shrinks into the amber die as the package draws on around it, with its grey 'generic GPU' tag. On 'compute die', label 'The chip' appears above the die with a small grey '= compute die' beside it. On 'the part that calculates', the first line beneath lands in amber: 'does the arithmetic'. On 'a thousandth', the second line lands in grey, 'holds almost nothing', and a magnifier over the die shows a small tray, tag '≈ 0.1 GB in all · ≈ 1/1,000 of the model', the same figure as earlier.

beats.say: The memory beside it, separate silicon, holds all seventy billion weights and does no arithmetic. A bus, a bundle of wires, joins them.
beats.show: The magnifier closes. The coral memory blocks light up; label 'The memory' with lines 'holds the weights' in coral and 'does no arithmetic' in grey. On 'separate silicon', a thin gap outline flashes between die and memory. On 'a bus', many thin parallel lines draw on from memory to die, tag 'bus = a bundle of wires'.

beats.say: So every weight crosses that bus, every token. That is the coral ninety-nine percent: moving the weights, and waiting for them.
beats.show: Coral weight tiles stream from the memory across the bus into the die, each flashing amber and vanishing as it is used; the memory never empties. Counter: 'token 1'; the full stream crosses; 'token 2'; it crosses again in full; 'token 3'. Tag under the bus: '140 GB, every token'. On 'the coral ninety-nine percent', the parked bar at the top-right brightens and slides a little toward centre and its '?' dissolves. On 'moving the weights', the blank name box fills with 'moving the weights'. On 'waiting for them', a thin coral leader line joins the tag to the flow on the bus.

beats.say: Were they in one place, there'd be no memory wall, and no need for this series.
beats.show: On 'one place', a ghost copy of the memory slides onto the die and the stream stops. On 'no memory wall', the ghost fades, the real memory stays where it was and the stream resumes; the bus band thickens into a translucent coral wall standing between die and memory, label 'the memory wall'. On 'no need for this series', the camera pushes into the bus until one wire fills the frame, handing over to the next scene.

scenes.name: bits, bytes, and a hundred and forty gigabytes
scenes.visual: One wire drawn as an oscilloscope trace on a dark grid, time running left to right, then the bits it carries assembled into bytes, a weight and the model. Left half: a ten-level trace with ten faint threshold bands labelled 0 to 9, heading 'ten levels?'. Right half: a two-level trace with two blue bands, 'high = 1' and 'low = 0', heading 'two levels'. Both bands are blue because they are neutral data; teal appears only on the tick that shows a reading survived. The same noise is applied to both traces, so the left one is misread and the right one survives. Later the right trace's readout lifts into a row of blue bit cells, then two coral byte blocks, then an equation in the bottom band. Earlier elements dim, not clear, as each new one lands.

beats.say: What crosses is bits, single yes-or-no signals, each a voltage on a wire. Ten levels could hold a digit, but telling ten apart, billions of times a second, on a warm chip, is far too hard.
beats.show: Left half: the trace steps between ten levels; readout above it '7 2 9 4'. On 'a warm chip', a thermometer icon at the top warms from blue to orange and the trace picks up a jitter. The level meant to be 7 sags into the band for 6; the readout's '7' turns grey, is struck through and becomes '6'. It happens again to the 4.

beats.say: Two levels, called one and zero, tolerate noise: a one can sag a long way and still read correctly. So every number is built from them, for engineering reasons, not mathematical ones, and counted in bits.
beats.show: Right half: the two-level trace with blue bands 'high = 1' and 'low = 0'. The same jitter is applied. On 'sag a long way', the high level droops to about two thirds of its height and the readout still shows '1', with a small teal tick 'read correctly'. Readout along the top: '1 0 1 1 0'. On 'engineering reasons', a grey tag: 'an engineering choice, not a mathematical one'. On 'counted in bits', the left half fades out.

beats.say: Eight bits make a byte, and a weight takes two bytes, enough for useful accuracy. So seventy billion weights become a hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: The readout lifts off the trace and becomes blue cells. On 'Eight bits', one cell first, label '1 bit = one yes-or-no', then on 'a byte' the row grows to eight cells reading 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1, a bracket draws under it 'one byte', and a small grey counter doubles beside it to '256 patterns'. On 'two bytes', two coral blocks slide together: '1 weight = 2 bytes = 16 bits', small grey '65,536 patterns'. Each label dims as the next lands. On 'seventy billion', the bit and byte labels fade and the bottom band builds '70 billion weights × 2 bytes = 140 GB' term by term, with a small grey note '1 GB = 1 billion bytes'. A coral file icon '140 GB' drops toward a tiny amber chip outline, bounces off, and settles into a large coral memory block: tag 'only fits in the memory'.

beats.say: Sixteen bits is the usual choice, and shrinking it comes later in the series. Parameters times bytes gives bytes. You'll use that constantly.
beats.show: Grey side tag in two lines: '16 bits: the common default' and 'fewer bits: later in the series'. On 'Parameters times bytes', everything else dims and the centre reads, in white with 'bytes' in coral: 'parameters × bytes each = bytes'.

scenes.name: bandwidth is width times frequency
scenes.visual: Top band: an equation in two lines, 'bandwidth =' over 'wires × bits per second per wire', with '÷ 8 → bytes per second' added at the end. A small clock icon labelled 'frequency' and a bracket labelled 'width' flank it. Below, two horizontal pipes run left to right with coral bit particles flowing in parallel lanes. Lane counts are drawn to scale, one lane standing for 64 wires: the upper laptop pipe has 2 lanes, the lower H100 pipe 80 hairline lanes, so the lower pipe is forty times taller. Particle speed per lane is almost the same in both: the lower pipe's particles move at about 87% of the upper's speed (5.2 against 6 billion bits a second), so the difference in total flow comes from the lane count alone. Each pipe has a bytes-per-second counter at its right end. In the last beat the pipes shrink to a corner and the GPU package from scene 2 returns.

beats.say: Bits cross at a rate called bandwidth. It's not speed in the everyday sense, but width times frequency: how many wires, times how often each sends a bit.
beats.show: Top band: 'bandwidth' appears in coral. On 'width', a bracket labelled 'width' appears to its left; on 'frequency', a ticking clock icon labelled 'frequency' to its right. On 'how many wires', the equation builds in two lines: 'bandwidth =' then 'wires × bits per second per wire', each term lighting as it is spoken. Then '÷ 8 → bytes per second' lands at the end in coral.

beats.say: A laptop's memory is a narrow pipe running fast. Not much gets through, about a hundred gigabytes a second.
beats.show: Upper pipe draws on, thin, 2 lanes, coral particles racing. Labels '≈ 128 wires' and '≈ 6 billion bits/s each'. The counter at its right end runs to '≈ 96 GB/s', then rounds to '≈ 100 GB/s'. Grey tag 'typical laptop, rounded'. Caption 'narrow pipe, running fast'.

beats.say: The H one hundred's is a wide pipe running steadily: five thousand one hundred and twenty wires, each a little slower, for three point three five terabytes per second.
beats.show: On 'wide pipe', the upper pipe's labels '≈ 128 wires' and '≈ 6 billion bits/s each', its 'typical laptop, rounded' tag and its caption dim to 30%, and the equation in the top band, with 'width' and 'frequency', dims to 40%; the upper counter '≈ 100 GB/s' stays bright for comparison. The lower pipe draws on, forty times taller, 80 hairline lanes, blue outline, particles a touch slower than above. Caption on the pipe: 'wide pipe, running steadily'. Labels '5,120 wires' and '≈ 5.2 billion bits/s each'. On 'five thousand one hundred and twenty wires', a tag between the pipes: '40× the wires → ≈ 35× the bandwidth'. The counter runs to '3.35 TB/s'. On 'each a little slower', a second caption lands beneath the pipe: 'far more, at about the same clock'. As the counter lands, the '40×' tag fades and a small grey tag replaces it: 'lanes to scale: 1 lane = 64 wires'.

beats.say: Memory gets faster mostly by getting wider, and that many wires can't be long, so it sits against the chip. Why it's hard to make faster comes later.
beats.show: On 'getting wider', the equation brightens again and the word 'wires' in it is underlined in teal. On 'can't be long', the pipes shrink into the bottom-left corner; the GPU package returns at centre with its 'generic GPU' tag, its bus redrawn as thousands of hair-thin lines, and the coral memory blocks slide inward until they nearly touch the amber die. Label 'wide needs short'. On 'hard to make faster', a small grey tag on the equation: 'why it's hard: later this chapter'.

scenes.name: close is not the same as on
scenes.visual: Opens on the previous scene's end state, the package with memory hugging the die. Heading 'Why the memory is not on the chip'. Three cards across the top band: amber 'Fast logic · one kind of silicon process', coral 'Dense storage · a different one', blue in two lines 'Nobody has made both' / 'work on one piece of silicon'. Below them, a postage stamp icon with the amber die drawn on it beside a coral '140 GB' block that grows many times larger. The shot ends by pulling back to the package and pushing into the hairline gap between die and memory, which is labelled 'the memory wall'.

beats.say: Why not put the memory on the chip? Each chip is optimised for one job. Logic and storage need different manufacturing processes, and nobody has made both work well on one piece of silicon.
beats.show: A ghost arrow tries to drag a coral memory stack onto the amber die; it springs back. Heading appears. The package dims to the background. On 'Logic', the amber card slides in at the left; on 'storage', the coral card at the middle, each with a small recipe-card icon labelled 'process', visibly different. On 'nobody has made both', the blue card lands at the right; the amber and coral cards slide together into one slab, a crack runs across it, and they separate again.

beats.say: And there isn't room. A hundred and forty gigabytes won't fit on a postage stamp of silicon, at any price.
beats.show: The three cards dim. Below them: a postage stamp icon with the amber die drawn on it. A coral block '140 GB' grows beside it until it dwarfs the stamp. A price-tag icon sits to the right of the stamp with a grey label 'at any price' beside it. On 'at any price', the price-tag icon spins up dollar signs, then a grey strike-through crosses the price-tag icon only; the label stays unstruck.

beats.say: So the memory sits off the chip, as close as possible, across the widest bus that can be built. Close is not the same as on, and that difference is the memory wall.
beats.show: Cards and stamp slide off. The camera pulls back to the GPU package filling the frame: coral stacks hugging the amber die, thousands of fine bus lines between them, tag 'off-chip: separate chips, side by side'. On 'Close is not the same as on', the camera pushes into the hairline gap between the die and one stack; label 'close ≠ on', which then becomes 'the memory wall'.

beats.say: It's not an oversight anyone could have avoided. It follows from what silicon can and cannot do.
beats.show: Hold on the gap. On 'not an oversight', a grey caption lands beneath: 'not an oversight anyone could avoid'. On 'what silicon can and cannot do', a second grey line: 'what silicon can and cannot do'.

scenes.name: latency is not bandwidth
scenes.visual: Two horizontal lanes, left to right. Top lane, heading 'Latency: how long one request takes': a blue 'ask' pill at the left, a long dashed 'wait' segment with a stopwatch above it, and a blue 'arrive' pill at the right. Bottom lane, heading 'Bandwidth: how much travels at once': parallel tracks carrying coral packets. Midway, the lanes slide down and two icons take the stage, a container ship (Fluent Emoji Flat 'ship') and a motorbike courier (Fluent Emoji Flat 'motor scooter'). At the end the bottom tracks are shown first running dry, then filled solid. Teal is used only for the fix, 'many in flight'.

beats.say: Every request the chip sends to memory makes a trip. How long one takes, from ask to arrive, is latency. Bandwidth is how much travels at once.
beats.show: Top lane: on 'sends to memory', a small amber chip outline at the left edge emits a blue pill 'ask'; a dashed segment stretches right with a stopwatch counting above it; on 'arrive', a blue pill 'arrive' lands at the right end. Heading 'Latency: how long one request takes'. On 'Bandwidth', the bottom lane draws six parallel coral tracks filled with packets moving at the same pace as the top lane, and an arrivals counter at the right end ticks up six at a time. On 'at once', the six tracks become twelve and the arrivals counter doubles its pace, while the top lane's wait stays exactly as long. Heading 'Bandwidth: how much travels at once'.

beats.say: They're independent. A container ship takes weeks but carries a town's goods: high bandwidth, high latency. A motorbike courier is the reverse.
beats.show: The lanes slide down and dim. Left: the container ship stacked with crates, tags 'latency: weeks' in grey and 'bandwidth: huge' in coral. Right, on 'motorbike courier': the motorbike with one parcel, tags 'latency: minutes' and 'bandwidth: tiny'. Caption: 'independent · wide and slow, narrow and quick'.

beats.say: Memory can't be made low-latency: distance and physics are what they are. But enough memory requests in flight keep the pipe from running dry.
beats.show: Icons leave; the lanes return. The top lane's wait is tagged 'fixed by distance'. On 'memory requests in flight', the bottom tracks first send one packet at a time, each waiting for the last to arrive, so the tracks are mostly empty: grey tag 'one at a time: runs dry'. Then requests launch back to back and the tracks fill solid: teal tag 'many in flight: stays full'. The top lane's wait never gets shorter.

beats.say: Confusing the two produces most of the wrong intuitions in this field. Hold them apart.
beats.show: Everything fades except two words with a deliberate gap between them: 'latency' in grey, 'bandwidth' in coral. On 'Hold them apart', the gap widens slightly.

scenes.name: a rate times a time gives an amount
scenes.visual: Centre: a fraction, 'bytes' over 'second', with the word 'per' sitting on the fraction bar. Then a coral pipe labelled '3.35 TB/s' pours into a tall bucket while a stopwatch above it runs to 0.03 s; the bucket's fill line stops at about 100 GB, below a dashed target line at 140 GB. Bottom band: two equation cards side by side, a multiplication and a division, joined by a bracket showing they reach the same verdict.

beats.say: A rate is an amount divided by a time: bytes per second, where per does the dividing. So a rate times a time gives back an amount.
beats.show: Heading 'a rate = amount ÷ time'. Blue box 'bytes' above a horizontal bar, blue box 'second' below it. The word 'per' appears on the bar, then morphs into a plain division line. On 'rate times a time', the heading rewrites to 'rate × time = amount' and the fraction slides to the top-left.

beats.say: Give the H one hundred our thirty milliseconds, a figure from the faster H two hundred. Three point three five terabytes a second, times thirty milliseconds, is about a hundred gigabytes.
beats.show: Grey tag at the top: 'what-if: the 30 ms came from the H200'. A coral pipe labelled '3.35 TB/s' pours into a tall bucket. A stopwatch above runs from '0' to '0.03 s = 30 ms' and the flow stops when it does. The equation builds beneath: '3.35 TB/s × 0.03 s = 100.5 GB'. The bucket's fill line is labelled '≈ 100 GB'.

beats.say: Not the hundred and forty needed: the whole story in one line of arithmetic. The earlier division says it from the other side: forty-two milliseconds, not thirty.
beats.show: A dashed line on the bucket, '140 GB needed', sits well above the fill; the gap is shaded coral, '≈ 40 GB short', with a small grey tag '100.5 ÷ 140 ≈ 72%'. On 'from the other side', the bucket and its tags, the equation under it, the heading, the parked fraction and the what-if tag all dim to 30%. Two cards build in the bottom band, each under a small grey header: left, header 'rate × time', card '3.35 TB/s × 30 ms ≈ 100 GB < 140 GB'; right, on 'forty-two milliseconds', header 'amount ÷ rate', card '140 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 41.8 ms > 30 ms'. A bracket joins them underneath: 'short by ×1.39, either way'.

scenes.name: reading a specification sheet
scenes.visual: A specification sheet, centre, drawn as a printed page with a document icon (Phosphor 'file-text') in its corner and heading 'H100'. Four rows land one by one, each with a name at the left, a value pill (a rounded label, not a chip icon) in the middle and a tag at the right reading 'an amount' or 'a rate'. Value pills are coloured by meaning: capacity blue, bandwidth coral, compute amber, power grey. Each row's side note shows only while that row is being spoken, then fades, so no more than five text items are bright at once. Later the capacity and bandwidth rows lift out, and a coral '140 GB' block is tested against the capacity row and overflows.

beats.say: Every specification is an amount or a rate, and keeping them apart is most of the skill. Take the H one hundred's sheet.
beats.show: Two tags at the top: blue 'an amount: gigabytes' and coral 'a rate: gigabytes per second'. On 'Take the H one hundred's sheet', the sheet slides in beneath them, heading 'H100', rows still empty.

beats.say: Memory capacity, eighty gigabytes: an amount. Bandwidth: a rate. Peak compute, nine hundred and eighty-nine teraflops, trillion operations a second: a rate. Power, seven hundred watts, energy per second: a rate too.
beats.show: Rows land on their names, and each earlier row dims slightly as the next arrives. Row 1: 'Memory capacity' · blue pill '80 GB' · tag 'an amount'. Row 2: 'Memory bandwidth' · coral pill '3.35 TB/s' · tag 'a rate'. Row 3: 'Peak compute' · amber pill '989 TFLOP/s' · tag 'a rate', side note '16-bit · 989 trillion ≈ 10¹⁵'. Row 4: 'Power draw' · grey pill '700 W' · tag 'a rate', side note 'watt = energy per second'. As row 4 lands, the three 'a rate' tags glow together, then the single 'an amount' tag glows: 'three rates, one amount'.

beats.say: Confusing capacity with bandwidth is the most common error. Capacity says whether the model fits. Bandwidth says how fast it's read once it does. A chip can fail either.
beats.show: The other rows dim. The capacity row and the bandwidth row lift out of the sheet and stand side by side, larger. Under capacity, a container icon and 'does it fit?'. Under bandwidth, a pipe icon and 'how fast is it read?'. On 'fail either', a grey tag between them: 'separate limits'.

beats.say: Ours fails the first: a hundred and forty gigabytes won't fit in eighty, so it needs two chips. Every number ahead comes off a sheet like this, and telling amount from rate sorts most claims.
beats.show: On 'a hundred and forty gigabytes', a coral block '140 GB' drops into the '80 GB' container and overflows its rim. On 'two chips', tag '140 ÷ 80 = 1.75 → at least 2 chips' and, smaller, 'splitting: later in the series'. On 'a sheet like this', the rows return to the sheet, which re-forms whole with all four tags lit.

scenes.name: the two specifications that matter
scenes.visual: Two large cards side by side in the top half: left amber 'Compute throughput', right coral 'Memory bandwidth'. Below them, two timeline lanes for one token on an H100, drawn to one scale from 0 to 45 ms at 30 px per ms: an amber lane that is a 4 px sliver at 0.14 ms, about a seventh of a millisecond, and a coral lane 1,254 px long to 41.8 ms. The coral lane is drawn as a run of slices, each followed by a tiny amber tick, to show the two overlapping. A white 'token done' marker lands at the end of the longer lane; a dashed ghost marker at the average is shown and struck out.

beats.say: Two lines matter most: compute throughput, operations per second, and memory bandwidth, bytes per second from memory. A token needs both: fetch the weights, and multiply them.
beats.show: The sheet's compute and bandwidth rows grow into the two cards. Left: amber 'Compute throughput', sub-line 'operations per second'. Right: coral 'Memory bandwidth', sub-lines 'bytes per second' and 'off-chip memory → chip'. On 'fetch', a coral arrow runs from the right card into the left; on 'multiply', an amber loop arrow circles on the left card.

beats.say: Pretend the model fits on one H one hundred. Its arithmetic takes about a seventh of a millisecond. Reading the weights, forty-two milliseconds.
beats.show: On 'Pretend', grey tag 'one token · H100 · if it fitted'. A time axis from 0 to 45 ms draws under the cards. On 'a seventh of a millisecond', the amber lane appears: '140 billion ops ÷ 989 trillion/s ≈ 0.14 ms', its bar a sliver at the far left. On 'Reading the weights', the coral lane grows from the left to almost the full width: '140 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 41.8 ms'. A small coral tag rides on it: 'moving the weights', the same name as the coral bar from earlier.

beats.say: They overlap: while one slice of weights is multiplied, the next is on its way. The slower one sets the pace and leaves the other idle, here the arithmetic. Forty-two milliseconds, not an average of twenty-one.
beats.show: On 'one slice of weights is multiplied', the coral lane splits into slices, each drawn faintly as a block of weight tiles, and the amber work redistributes as a tiny amber tick under the end of each slice, ticks and slices advancing together. On 'The slower one sets the pace', a white vertical marker 'token done ≈ 42 ms' drops at the end of the coral lane, and a small grey tag between the cards reads 'slower one sets the pace'. On 'leaves the other idle, here the arithmetic', the amber card greys out with a small hourglass icon and tag 'idle, waiting'. On 'not an average', a dashed ghost marker at '≈ 21 ms · average' appears at 630 px, then a grey strike-through crosses it out.

beats.say: Two independent resources. Almost every performance question from here on asks which one a workload runs out of first.
beats.show: The lanes fade; the two cards remain, with a question between them in white: 'which runs out first?'

scenes.name: one lever against three ceilings
scenes.visual: Top band: one amber card, 'Compute: transistor density', with an arrow climbing from it up and off the top of the frame. Bottom band: three coral cards in a row joined by '×' signs, 'rate per pin', 'pins per stack', 'stacks per chip', each later capped by a dashed ceiling line just above it. Right edge: the GPU package from scene 2, which as it zooms swaps its grey 'generic GPU' tag for a blue label 'H100 · 80 GB', zoomed so the memory reads as towers of thin layers. It shows six memory sites around the die, five coral and one grey, because the H100 package has six sites with five in use. Left of the top band, a small inset of the amber worker grid from scene 1 appears for the first beat only. Earlier tags dim as later ones land.

beats.say: They also grow at different speeds. Transistors are the tiny switches arithmetic is built from, and compute scales with how densely they're packed. No hard ceiling yet.
beats.show: Top band: amber card 'Compute scales with one thing' over a smaller amber card 'transistor density'. On 'tiny switches', a small inset of the amber worker grid from scene 1, about 6 by 4 squares, fades in beside the transistor-density card. On 'densely', one square of the inset subdivides into four, then sixteen squares in the same area. An arrow climbs from the card, tag 'no hard ceiling reached yet'; the inset fades.

beats.say: Bandwidth is a product of three. The memory comes in stacks, towers of layers, wired to the chip through pins: rate per pin, times pins per stack, times stacks.
beats.show: The compute tag dims. Right edge: the package zooms in and its grey 'generic GPU' tag changes to the blue label 'H100 · 80 GB'; coral towers of thin layers sit around the amber die, one site grey. A pointer labels one tower 'stack'; grey tag 'H100: 5 active stacks'. On 'pins', a close-up shows a dense field of fine connections under one stack. On 'rate per pin, times pins per stack, times stacks', the three coral cards build left to right with '×' between them.

beats.say: The H one hundred's five stacks of one thousand and twenty-four pins are the five thousand one hundred and twenty wires from earlier.
beats.show: Numbers drop into the cards: '5' into 'stacks per chip' on 'five stacks', '1,024' into 'pins per stack' on 'one thousand and twenty-four', and '≈ 5.23 Gbit/s' into 'rate per pin'. On 'five thousand one hundred and twenty wires', the label '5,120 wires' from the bandwidth scene flies in and splits into '1,024 × 5'. A result line slides in beneath, in coral: '5.23 Gbit/s × 5,120 ≈ 26.8 trillion bits/s ÷ 8 ≈ 3.35 TB/s'.

beats.say: Each term has a ceiling. Pins switch only so fast before high and low blur. Only so many connections fit under a stack. And the package has edges. So memory is hard to make much faster.
beats.show: The result line and the stack tag dim. A dashed ceiling line drops over each coral card on its phrase. On 'switch only so fast': over card 1, a tiny voltage trace whose clean high and low edges smear together, tag 'signal integrity'. On 'connections fit under a stack': over card 2, the dense field of dots under one stack, tag 'only so many fit'. On 'the package has edges': over card 3, the package outline with stacks crowding the edges, tag 'package edges'. On 'hard to make much faster', the three dashed ceilings flash together and a small grey tag lands under the cards: 'why memory is hard to speed up'.

beats.say: Compute keeps climbing. Bandwidth fights three ceilings set by geometry and physics, not lack of effort. That's the memory wall's mechanism: one lever against three.
beats.show: On 'Compute keeps climbing', the amber arrow keeps rising past the top of the frame. On 'three ceilings', the three coral cards press up against their dashed ceilings and stop. Heading: 'one lever vs three ceilings'. On 'the memory wall's mechanism', the text resolves to amber '1 lever' and coral '3 constrained levers'.

scenes.name: the divergence, measured
scenes.visual: An XY chart filling the centre. Horizontal axis: years, '2012' at the left, '2022' at the right. Vertical axis: growth since 2012 on a log scale, 300 px per factor of ten, gridlines at '1×', '10×' and '100×', so equal steps up mean equal multiplications. Steady percentage growth is a straight line on this axis: an amber line for compute rises to 80× (571 px above the base) and a coral line for bandwidth to 17× (369 px), both from one shared dot at the bottom-left. On a log axis the vertical gap between the two tips is their ratio, 4.7× (202 px), so a double arrow there is honest. Grey corner tag: 'schematic curves, real endpoints'.

beats.say: Across one decade of top-tier server G P Us, on a log axis where each step multiplies, compute rose about eighty times.
beats.show: Axes draw on. On 'one decade', horizontal-axis labels '2012' and '2022' land at its two ends. On 'log axis', horizontal gridlines at '1×', '10×' and '100×' on the vertical axis, 300 px apart, land and a small note appears: 'each step up: ×10'. A white dot sits at '2012, 1×' and splits into an amber and a coral dot. On 'eighty times', the amber line rises steadily to the top-right, label 'compute, ×80'.

beats.say: Off-chip bandwidth rose about seventeen times. Eighty over seventeen is about four point seven.
beats.show: On 'seventeen times', the coral line rises at a gentler slope, label 'bandwidth, ×17'. Small tags ride on the lines: amber '≈ +55% a year', coral '≈ +33% a year'. On 'eighty over seventeen', a vertical double-headed arrow spans the gap between the two tips at 2022, label '80 ÷ 17 ≈ 4.7×' and, smaller, 'arithmetic per byte delivered'.

beats.say: The curves are schematic, the endpoints real, and still spreading. One decade moved the balance by almost a factor of five.
beats.show: The grey corner tag 'schematic curves, real endpoints' brightens. On 'still spreading', both lines extend past 2022 as dashed lines, still pulling apart, the gap between them visibly widening. On 'almost a factor of five', the '4.7×' label pulses once.

scenes.name: a name and a date
scenes.visual: A horizontal timeline across the middle: '1995' at the left, '2017' near the middle, 'today' at the right. A blue card at 1995 with a paper icon (Phosphor 'article'): 'Wulf and McKee, 1995', small title 'Hitting the Memory Wall'. A blue pill at 2017: 'the transformer'. A thin coral band runs the whole length of the timeline, labelled 'the gap, always there'. A coral card at the right end: 'What changed'. At the end, three small icons gather on the band and a small walking-figure icon tagged 'AI' walks into it. Earlier cards dim as later ones land.

beats.say: Two computer architects, Wulf and McKee, named the memory wall in nineteen ninety-five, more than twenty years before the transformer, the design today's language models use.
beats.show: The timeline draws left to right. At '1995', the blue card lands: 'Wulf and McKee, 1995', with the paper icon and small title 'Hitting the Memory Wall'. On 'the transformer', a blue pill lands at '2017': 'the transformer'. A bracket spans 1995 to 2017, label '22 years'.

beats.say: What changed is the workload, not the hardware trend. The gap was always there. Now a computation hungry enough for bytes makes it the dominant concern.
beats.show: Coral card at the right end: 'What changed' over two lines, 'not the hardware trend,' and 'the workload'. On 'always there', the thin coral band draws along the full timeline from 1995, label 'the gap, always there'. On 'dominant concern', a small tag under the card: 'not one concern among many'.

beats.say: Language-model inference is among the most byte-hungry workloads ever built.
beats.show: The 1995 card and 2017 pill dim. Above 'today', a gauge labelled 'hunger for bytes' swings to its coral end; tag under it 'language-model inference'. A coral pill label '140 GB per token' pins beside the gauge.

beats.say: That's the memory wall: arithmetic waiting on memory, because the two live apart and the gap between their speeds keeps growing.
beats.show: The gauge dims. On 'That's the memory wall', the coral band's label changes from 'the gap, always there' to 'the memory wall'. Three small icons then settle on the band as their words are spoken: on 'arithmetic waiting', an amber hourglass; on 'live apart', a tiny package with a gap between die and memory; on 'keeps growing', a tiny pair of diverging lines, amber and coral.

beats.say: Not an A I problem hardware failed to anticipate, but a long-standing trend A I walked straight into.
beats.show: On 'long-standing trend', the band glows along its full length back to 1995. On 'walked straight into', a small walking-figure icon tagged 'AI' enters from the right and walks into the band, stopping against it. Hold.

scenes.name: the line to remember
scenes.visual: One continuous shot. Four small tiles, miniatures of earlier scenes, sit in a dim row along the bottom: the amber worker grid, the bus with coral weight flow, three coral cards under dashed ceilings, the two diverging lines. Two large empty card outlines draw side by side in the centre, amber on the left and coral on the right, and fill on the final line: 'Arithmetic · cheap' and 'Data movement · expensive'. Nothing else is on screen at the end.

beats.say: Every decision in production inference, and every paper in this series, takes one line as given. If you remember one thing, make it this. Everything after is working out what it implies.
beats.show: On 'Every decision', the four recap tiles slide up from the bottom edge in a row, then dim. On 'every paper in this series', a small stack of paper icons slides in at the end of the row and dims with the tiles. On 'one line', two empty card outlines draw themselves in the centre, amber on the left, coral on the right. On 'remember one thing', a soft glow builds behind them. Nothing else moves.

beats.say: Arithmetic is cheap. Data movement is expensive.
beats.show: On 'Arithmetic is cheap', the amber card fills: 'Arithmetic' with 'cheap' beneath. On 'Data movement is expensive', the coral card fills: 'Data movement' with 'expensive' beneath. Hold both for two seconds before the chapter ends.
